svg.aria-label: Diagram: how Google Cloud selects a route as a staged elimination in which special paths, policy-based routes, subnet routes and Private Service Connect endpoints can each end evaluation outright; why longest-prefix matching applies at only one stage and only to static and dynamic routes; the three stages resolved by an undocumented internal algorithm and the single remedy of unique priorities; and the final stage where ECMP does not cross preference categories and is not guaranteed to be flow-consistent
svg.title: Routing order: an elimination with one longest-prefix stage, three internal tie-breaks, and non-sticky ECMP
svg.text: Route selection is an elimination, not a comparison. Several stages can end it outright.
Longest prefix applies at exactly one stage, and only to static and dynamic routes.
The order, and which stages end it outright
1 SPECIAL PATHS — if one applies, the model contains ONLY it. Evaluation stops.
2 POLICY-BASED — by priority alone. A match delivers to its load balancer and
disregards every non-policy-based route.
3 SUBNET ROUTES — a match is EXCLUSIVE. All other routes disregarded; stop.
4 PSC endpoints for global Google APIs — a match sends to a Google Front End; stop.
5 onward — only now are static and dynamic routes considered at all.
Where longest prefix applies, and where it does not
MOST SPECIFIC DESTINATION is one stage, and it only sees static and dynamic routes:
10.240.1.0/24 is a more specific destination than 10.240.0.0/16.
It does NOT govern policy-based routes. Those go by priority alone, and the route chosen
might not be the most specific match for the packet source or destination.
Nor subnet routes — those win by matching at all, and specificity never enters it.
Three stages decided by an internal algorithm
Tied highest-priority POLICY-BASED routes — one is chosen by an internal algorithm.
PEERING custom routes from two or more peers — one peer network chosen internally, and
the choice may change when you add or remove any peering.
NCC dynamic routes from two or more routing VPC networks — spokes chosen internally.
The documented remedy is the same each time: GIVE THE ROUTES UNIQUE PRIORITIES.
Priority is not a preference here. It is how you stop the platform guessing.
The last stage, and the trap inside it
ECMP does not cross PREFERENCE CATEGORIES: instance and Classic VPN next hops first,
then dynamic routes of one type, then a single internal passthrough NLB, then
default-internet-gateway last. No ECMP across those bands, and none across NLB hops.
ECMP IS NOT FLOW-CONSISTENT. Five-tuple hash with ports, three-tuple without — and
consistent next hop selection for a given hash IS NOT GUARANTEED, even unchanged.
So a stateful next hop — a NAT or firewall VM — can see a flow move mid-connection.
Two different drops, and the difference is diagnostic: an empty model returns ICMP type 3
code 0 unreachable; a subnet route matching an unused address or stopped VM drops silently.
And a next hop can be valid to the platform and dead inside: Google Cloud does not validate
whether the guest OS of a next hop VM is processing packets. Reachable is not the same as up.
